summary: Announces that the London node of the ARPANET has been connected since early September. It consists of a TIP and a local PDP-9 Host that front-ends the Rutherford High Energy Laboratory's IBM 360/195, linked to it by a 2.4 kbps line.

plainLanguage.summary: The network reached London. A small computer there lets people in England use a big research computer through the network.

subtitle: The ARPANET reaches London with a node at the University of London

tldr.problem: In early 1973, ARPANET had no presence in the United Kingdom, limiting access for UK researchers.
tldr.mechanism: A TIP (Terminal Interface Processor) and PDP-9 host were installed at the University of London Institute of Computer Science, with the PDP-9 front-ending the Rutherford High Energy Laboratory's IBM 360/195 computer 60 miles away via a 2.4 Kbps line.
tldr.outcome: UK researchers could now use ARPANET to access the Rutherford 360, which offered capabilities in network measurements, high energy physics and accelerator design. The host was available for limited experimental use with a free guest account.

today: RFC 588 documents the opening of ARPANET's London node. This was an important milestone in ARPANET's internationalization. The IBM 360/195 at Rutherford is long since retired, and this node is no longer in operation, but it represented early progress in connecting research communities across the Atlantic via packet switching.

sections.title: London Connects to ARPANET
sections.content:
Since early September 1973, the London node of the ARPANET (network address 42) has been online. It consists of a TIP (Terminal Interface Processor, address 170) and a local PDP-9 host computer (address 0) running at the University of London Institute of Computer Science (ULICS).

The PDP-9 serves as a front-end to the Rutherford High Energy Laboratory's IBM 360/195, located 60 miles from London and connected via a 2.4 Kbps (kilobits per second) line. This arrangement lets users in London access the large 360 computer for remote job entry and interactive work over the network.
sections.plainLanguage: London got connected to the ARPANET through a small computer that talks to a big research computer 60 miles away.

sections.title: The IBM 360/195 and Available Resources
sections.content:
The Rutherford 360/195 is a substantial machine for the era, with 2 megabytes of fast store (750 nanosecond memory), a fixed-head disk, and many peripherals. It runs IBM's OS/MVT operating system release 21.7, HASP II (a job entry and spooling system) version 3.1, and a locally written message switching system called MAST plus an interactive editor called ELECTRIC. The system supports about 20 remote workstations, many of which are GEC 2050s simulating IBM 1130s.

Users connect via Telnet to the PDP-9, which simulates an IBM 1130 terminal with two card readers, two card punches, two line printers and three MAST consoles. The facility is available for limited experimental use. A free guest account (GUEST) is provided for demonstration, with a very limited allowance of 1 minute of CPU time per week and maximum job runtime of 10 seconds. Proper accounts for appropriate users can be arranged at no charge.
sections.plainLanguage: The 360 is a big research computer with lots of disk space and many attachments. Anyone can try a guest account with very limited time just to see what it does.

sections.title: Access and Availability
sections.content:
The London node is primarily available between 19:00 and 09:00 local time (19 hours ahead of the American West Coast, 5 hours ahead of the East Coast), with additional availability during daytime periods when users are in the computer room. No operator is present overnight, but messages sent during off-hours will be read and answered in the morning. Contact details are KIRSTEIN@ISI for account arrangements and network mail, AVS (the RFC author, A. V. Stokes) at the NIC, or Peter Higginson (PLH at NIC) for connection problems.

Of particular interest to the operators are applications in network measurements, high energy physics and accelerator design, though other cooperative projects involving a US group and interested UK parties would be considered. The intention is not to make the 360/195 a regular service host like other network computers, but rather a facility for collaborative projects.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer is mostly available at night London time (morning in California). UK scientists can use it for physics research or to work with American collaborators on network projects.

sections.title: Technical Protocols and Facilities
sections.content:
The PDP-9 has 16K 18-bit words of memory and a 256K-word drum for storage. It interfaces to the ARPANET using the IMP-HOST protocol (for talking to the ARPANET IMP), the HOST-HOST protocol (for talking to other hosts), the ICP (Initial Connection Protocol) for starting sessions, and the TELNET protocol for terminal interaction. The initial implementation allows Telnet login and access to the ELECTRIC editor for file entry, editing and submission to the batch stream, with interactive inspection of job output. RJE (Remote Job Entry) and FTP (File Transfer Protocol) implementations are planned.

Primitive help facilities are available on both the PDP-9 (via the %H command) and the 360 (via TYPE JB=HELP). A full help file is provided on the PDP-9 for users connecting for the first time.
sections.plainLanguage: The small computer uses all the standard network protocols to talk to other computers and handle remote login and file transfer.
